citations</a></li></ul></nav><div id="abstract" class="section level1" number="1">
<h1><span class="header-section-number">1</span> Abstract</h1>
<p>Missed hospital appointments create uncertainty in scheduling and can
leave capacity unused. This study analyses historical appointment
records and estimates attendance probabilities using Random Forest and
XGBoost. The working file contains 53,978 appointments before cleaning
and 53,976 afterward. Preparation includes checking records, correcting
target labels, converting dates and calculating waiting days. Patients
remain separate across training, validation and testing partitions.
Validation F1 selects follow-up thresholds, while test evaluation
includes precision, recall, F1 and Brier score. Random Forest obtains
test F1 0.4450 and XGBoost obtains 0.4468. The final demonstration
reports attending and missing probabilities for a fictional appointment.
The results support reminder prioritisation as a research prototype.
They do not establish that reminders improve attendance or that the
model transfers to other hospitals. Incomplete source coverage and the
absence of several personal and operational factors limit the
findings.</p>
</div>
<div id="introduction" class="section level1" number="2">
<h1><span class="header-section-number">2</span> Introduction</h1>
<div id="background" class="section level2" number="2.1">
<h2><span class="header-section-number">2.1</span> Background</h2>
<p>Hospital staff must plan appointments despite uncertainty about
patient attendance. Historical records can identify patterns and support
estimates of missed-appointment risk.</p>
</div>
<div id="problem-statement" class="section level2" number="2.2">
<h2><span class="header-section-number">2.2</span> Problem
statement</h2>
<p>How can historical patient and appointment information help identify
appointments at higher risk of being missed, while reporting the
probability of attendance?</p>
</div>
<div id="objectives" class="section level2" number="2.3">
<h2><span class="header-section-number">2.3</span> Objectives</h2>
<ol style="list-style-type: decimal">
<li>Prepare appointment records for analysis.</li>
<li>Compare attendance across age groups, gender, waiting periods and
SMS status.</li>
<li>Train Random Forest and XGBoost probability models.</li>
<li>Select follow-up thresholds using validation data and evaluate test
performance.</li>
<li>Demonstrate attending and missing probabilities for a new fictional
patient.</li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="scope" class="section level2" number="2.4">
<h2><span class="header-section-number">2.4</span> Scope</h2>
<p>The implementation analyses attendance and predicts outcomes. It does
not book, cancel or reschedule appointments, and it does not send SMS
messages. The SMS indicator must already be available at the time a
prediction is made.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="data" class="section level1" number="3">
<h1><span class="header-section-number">3</span> Data</h1>
<div id="source-and-variables" class="section level2" number="3.1">
<h2><span class="header-section-number">3.1</span> Source and
variables</h2>
<p>The working file is <code>KaggleV2-May-2016.csv</code>, associated
with the Medical Appointment No Shows dataset. Each row represents an
appointment; patients can appear more than once. Counts below describe
the imported working file, which may be a subset of the original
dataset.</p>

<th>Description</th>

</thead>

<tr class="odd">
<td><code>PatientId</code>, <code>AppointmentID</code></td>
<td>Patient and appointment identifiers</td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td><code>Gender</code>, <code>Age</code></td>
<td>Recorded demographic details</td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td><code>ScheduledDay</code>, <code>AppointmentDay</code></td>
<td>Booking and appointment dates</td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td><code>Neighbourhood</code></td>
<td>Recorded neighbourhood</td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td><code>Scholarship</code></td>
<td>Welfare programme indicator</td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td><code>Hipertension</code>, <code>Diabetes</code>,
<code>Alcoholism</code></td>
<td>Recorded health indicators</td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td><code>Handcap</code></td>
<td>Recorded disability category</td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td><code>SMS_received</code></td>
<td>Recorded SMS reminder indicator; does not prove reading</td>
</tr>
<tr class="odd">
<td><code>verification</code></td>
<td>Target renamed from No-show, recoded as Attended or Missed</td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td><code>WaitingDays</code></td>
<td>Appointment date minus booking date in calendar days</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>The original <strong>No-show = Yes</strong> means
<strong>Missed</strong>, while <strong>No</strong> means
<strong>Attended</strong>.</p>
</div>

<div id="methodology" class="section level1" number="4">
<h1><span class="header-section-number">4</span> Methodology</h1>
<div id="overall-workflow" class="section level2" number="4.1">
<h2><span class="header-section-number">4.1</span> Overall workflow</h2>
<ol style="list-style-type: decimal">
<li>Import and inspect the CSV.</li>
<li>Clean records and calculate waiting days.</li>
<li>Separate patients into training, validation and testing
partitions.</li>
<li>Fit Random Forest and XGBoost on model-training records.</li>
<li>Select thresholds on validation records.</li>
<li>Evaluate fixed models and thresholds on testing records.</li>
<li>Interpret attendance patterns and demonstrate a new appointment
prediction.</li>
<li>Save models, results and report data.</li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="data-cleaning" class="section level2" number="4.2">
<h2><span class="header-section-number">4.2</span> Data cleaning</h2>
<p>The notebook checks missing values, duplicate rows and data types. It
removes negative ages, converts date fields and excludes invalid waiting
periods. Age zero remains valid for infants. Repeated patients remain in
the dataset because separate appointments are legitimate
observations.</p>

<div id="training-validation-and-testing" class="section level2" number="4.4">
<h2><span class="header-section-number">4.4</span> Training validation
and testing</h2>
<p>Approximately 80% of patients enter the outer training partition. Of
those, approximately 20% enter validation. The remaining patients form
the test set. Appointment proportions differ because patients have
different record counts.</p>

<div id="models-and-evaluation" class="section level2" number="4.5">
<h2><span class="header-section-number">4.5</span> Models and
evaluation</h2>
<table>
<colgroup>
<col width="20%" />
<col width="44%" />
<col width="35%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr class="header">
<th>Model</th>
<th>Configuration</th>
<th>Evaluation</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr class="odd">
<td>Random Forest</td>
<td>300 trees, mtry 3, minimum node size 20, probability forest</td>
<td>Precision, recall, F1, accuracy, Brier score</td>
</tr>
<tr class="even">
<td>XGBoost</td>
<td>Binary logistic, eta 0.05, depth 4, child weight 10, row and column
sampling 0.8</td>
<td>Same test metrics; validation log loss for early stopping</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Both models use seed 33. XGBoost allows up to 500 rounds and stops
after 30 rounds without validation improvement. Thresholds from 0.01 to
0.99 maximise validation F1. The test set does not determine thresholds.
Random Forest uses the method implemented in <code>ranger</code> (Wright
and Ziegler, 2017); XGBoost follows the boosting system described by
Chen and Guestrin (2016).</p>
</div>
</div>

<p>Importance describes how a model uses features. It does not establish
causes or explain an individual prediction. The two importance scales
differ.</p>
</div>

prediction</h1>

outcome.</p>

<p>Attending and missing probabilities total approximately 100% after
rounding. The more probable outcome uses 50%, while the reminder flag
uses the selected validation threshold. Staff could use flags to
prioritise confirmation calls. This demonstration does not validate the
model or establish an operational benefit.</p>
</div>
<div id="model-comparison-and-discussion" class="section level1" number="9">
<h1><span class="header-section-number">9</span> Model comparison and
discussion</h1>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Random Forest:</strong> precision 31.60%, recall 75.22%,
F1 0.4450, Brier score 0.1516.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>XGBoost:</strong> precision 32.52%, recall 71.37%, F1
0.4468, Brier score 0.1505.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>The analysis addresses attendance patterns and implements both
probability models. Lower thresholds prioritise recall but create more
unnecessary calls. The confusion matrices quantify this workload. Small
differences in F1 do not establish a statistically reliable winner. The
new-patient output demonstrates the interface between patient details,
probability estimates and follow-up flags.</p>
</div>
<div id="limitations" class="section level1" number="10">
<h1><span class="header-section-number">10</span> Limitations</h1>
<ul>
<li>The working CSV may be a subset; its coverage must be
documented.</li>
<li>Patient-separated testing does not establish performance on future
dates or other hospitals.</li>
<li>Transport barriers, urgency and other relevant factors are
absent.</li>
<li>SMS status does not establish reading and must be known at
prediction time.</li>
<li>Threshold selection maximises F1 rather than hospital benefit or
call capacity.</li>
<li>Probability calibration and subgroup performance need further
assessment.</li>
<li>The test set was inspected during development; external evaluation
would provide stronger evidence.</li>
<li>Feature importance and descriptive graphs show associations, not
causation.</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="conclusion" class="section level1" number="11">
<h1><span class="header-section-number">11</span> Conclusion</h1>
<p>The project prepares appointment records, analyses attendance
patterns and fits Random Forest and XGBoost. Validation selects
follow-up thresholds, and test results quantify probability quality and
missed-appointment detection. The final output provides attending and
missing probabilities with a separate reminder flag. This is a research
prototype; practical use needs external validation and an assessment of
follow-up costs and benefits.</p>
<div id="future-work" class="section level2" number="11.1">
<h2><span class="header-section-number">11.1</span> Future work</h2>
<ul>
<li>Verify complete source coverage and evaluate later
appointments.</li>
<li>Assess calibration and performance across patient groups.</li>
<li>Choose thresholds according to reminder capacity and costs.</li>
<li>Add an input interface and test whether targeted reminders improve
attendance.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
<div id="reproducibility" class="section level1" number="12">
<h1><span class="header-section-number">12</span> Reproducibility</h1>
<p>This report renders saved experiment results without retraining
models. Keep <code>report_data.rds</code> beside the report. To
reproduce training, use the Colab notebook with the same CSV, split seed
and package versions. Saving results does not by itself create Git
history; version control must be maintained separately.</p>

analysis code.</p>
